Anselm of Canterbury
AN-selm uv KAN-ter-ber-ee
proper noun (medieval archbishop and theologian)
From Anselm (c. 1033–1109), an Italian monk who became Abbot of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury; the name from the Germanic ans (god) and helm (helmet, protection).

See also: Anselm of Canterbury

📖 Biblical Definition

Anselm of Canterbury was a medieval monk, abbot, and archbishop, one of the keenest minds of the age, whose chief labour was to give reasoned account of the faith he already believed—“faith seeking understanding.” The dictionary honours two of his enduring contributions. First, in his great work Cur Deus Homo (“Why God Became Man”) he set forth the satisfaction theory of the atonement: that sin is an infinite offence against the infinite majesty of God, that the debt could be paid by none but God yet must be paid by man, and that therefore the God-man alone could make satisfaction—a true forerunner of the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution, in which Christ bears the debt His people could never pay. Second, in the Proslogion he framed the ontological argument, reasoning from the very idea of God as “that than which nothing greater can be conceived” to His necessary existence. The dictionary receives these as honourable labours of a mind devoted to God, drawing out from Scripture and reason what the cross truly accomplished. Yet Anselm laboured within the medieval Roman church, and his piety was marked by its errors—a tender but mistaken devotion to the Virgin Mary, addressing prayers to her, and a sacramental and ecclesial framework that the Reformation would later test by the Word and find wanting in part. The dictionary applies its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition: honour the genuine insight into the cross and the rigour of his thought, while naming his Marian devotion and Roman setting as the error of his age. The seed of substitution he planted, the Reformers brought to its full harvest.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Medieval Archbishop of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109); honoured for the satisfaction theory of the atonement in Cur Deus Homo (a forerunner of penal substitution) and the ontological argument, with his Marian devotion and Roman setting named as error.

ANSELM OF CANTERBURY, proper noun. [From ans, god, and helm, protection.] A medieval monk, abbot, and archbishop (c. 1033–1109).

Famed for “faith seeking understanding” (fides quaerens intellectum).

In Cur Deus Homo he set the satisfaction theory of the atonement, a forerunner of penal substitution.

In the Proslogion he framed the ontological argument for God's existence.

Honoured for his insight, with his Marian devotion and Roman setting named as error.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Anselm laboured within the medieval Roman church; his satisfaction theory anticipated penal substitution, but his Marian devotion and Roman sacramental framework were the error of his age, corrected by the Reformation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the genuine good in Anselm: a mind of rare power consecrated to God, who gave the church the satisfaction theory of the atonement in Cur Deus Homo. Reasoning that sin is an infinite offence against an infinite God, that the debt must be paid by man yet can be paid only by God, he concluded that the God-man alone could satisfy—a true forerunner of the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution, in which Christ bears the punishment His people deserved. His ontological argument likewise stands as a serious labour of faith seeking understanding. These the dictionary receives with gratitude as honourable history.

Yet Anselm was a man of the medieval Roman church, and his piety carried its errors. He addressed prayers and tender devotion to the Virgin Mary, honouring the creature in ways Scripture reserves for God alone, for there is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. His sacramental and ecclesial framework belonged to a church the Reformation would later weigh by the Word and reform. Applying its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition, the dictionary honours the insight into the cross and the rigour of his thought while naming the Marian devotion and the Roman setting as the error of his age. The seed of satisfaction he planted, the Reformers brought to full harvest in justification by faith alone.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Germanic ans (god) and helm (helmet, protection); the name of the Archbishop of Canterbury whose Cur Deus Homo shaped the doctrine of the atonement.

expand to see more

Ans, Germanic, “god”; helm, “protection,” whence the name Anselm.

Abbot of Bec, later Archbishop of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109).

Cur Deus Homo, “Why God Became Man,” his treatise on the atonement.

Proslogion, the work setting forth the ontological argument.

Fides quaerens intellectum, “faith seeking understanding,” his motto.
